title: Scaling Hindi Quantum Natural Language Processing through Automatic Pregroup Supertagging
authors: Gautami Sanjay Naik, Krishna Bhatia, Mithun Paul Saint-Germain, H Aswath Babu
abstract: Quantum Natural Language Processing (QNLP) uses pregroup grammars to translate grammatical structure into diagrammatic representations and quantum circuits. Recent Hindi QNLP work has shown that Hindi-specific pregroup grammars can support grammar-sensitive compositional models, but grammatical type assignment is still largely manual, limiting scalability. This paper formulates automatic Hindi pregroup supertagging as a token-level classification task. Using a manually annotated corpus of 380 Hindi sentences, we evaluate lexical, contextual, prompting-based, lexical-repair, and suffix/morphology-aware methods. Results show that simple lexical and contextual models are strong in this low-resource setting: contextual backoff achieves the best completed accuracy of 64.56\%, while raw Qwen2.5 prompting reaches only 11.65\%. Lexical repair raises LLM-assisted prediction to 64.08\%, demonstrating the value of constraining generative outputs with symbolic grammar knowledge. Diagnostic analysis further shows that seen and unambiguous tokens are much easier than unseen tokens, and suffix/morphology features improve karaka-token accuracy but not overall performance. These results show that automatic Hindi pregroup assignment is feasible and can reduce reliance on manual annotation in future multilingual QNLP pipelines.
summary: This paper tackles the challenge of automatically tagging grammatical structures in Hindi to enable scalable Quantum Natural Language Processing (QNLP). By treating supertagging as a classification task, the authors compared various machine learning approaches. They found that while LLMs are powerful, they require explicit symbolic constraints, like lexical repair, to perform reliably, suggesting a path toward automating complex linguistic preprocessing.
main_problem: The paper addresses the bottleneck of manually assigning grammatical types (pregroup supertagging) required to scale Quantum Natural Language Processing (QNLP) for the Hindi language.
main_result: Contextual backoff models achieved the best performance (64.56%), significantly outperforming raw LLM prompting (11.65%), demonstrating that symbolic constraints are crucial for utility.
method: The task is framed as a token-level classification, comparing lexical, contextual, and LLM-assisted methods, including lexical repair, against a manually annotated corpus.
model_or_system: The underlying model is Quantum Natural Language Processing (QNLP), which uses pregroup grammars to map grammatical structure onto quantum circuits. The specific system involves Hindi language processing.
key_observables: Token-level exact-match accuracy, comparing performance across different feature sets (lexical, contextual, LLM-constrained).
important_parameters: The performance gap between seen/unambiguous tokens and unseen tokens, and the relative improvement gained by adding symbolic repair to LLM outputs.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that automatic supertagging is feasible, but the study notes the difficulty in handling unseen tokens and the necessity of symbolic constraints over raw generative power.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the pipeline for automatic Hindi pregroup supertagging. Table 1 compares various systems' performance, while Table 3 shows diagnostic results comparing performance on seen versus unseen tokens.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the QNLP framework and the manual annotation bottleneck, then formulates the problem as token-level classification. It evaluates multiple methods (lexical, contextual, LLM-based) and concludes by analyzing the strengths and limitations of each approach.
why_interesting: While not directly about quantum hardware or condensed matter physics, the work demonstrates the application of formal grammar structures (pregroup grammars) to computational linguistics, which shares conceptual parallels with structured representations used in quantum information theory.
